exhibits.question: How often are Anthropic and OpenAI putting out new models?
exhibits.heading: Anthropic and OpenAI put out a new model about every two weeks for a year
exhibits.after: Start with why your eyes are on the name at all, because while we watch the names, the setting that decides your answer gets chosen out of sight. Look at how often the names change. Anthropic, which makes Claude, launched Claude Opus 4.8 in May, Claude Opus 5 in July and Claude Opus 5.5 in September, with Sonnet, Fable and Haiku versions alongside. OpenAI's release notes climb from GPT-5.1 last November to GPT-6.1 Sol at the end of September. OpenAI even says a model will "generally remain available in ChatGPT for 90 days after a successor is released." Ninety days, and then the next name takes over.
exhibits.takeaway: Between them the two labs launched new models on at least 26 days in under a year, and six of those launches came in the 16 days from 22 September to 7 October 2026.

exhibits.question: Which changes the score more, a new model version or the thinking level, and what does each cost?
exhibits.heading: Turning up the thinking lifted Claude and GPT more than a new version did
exhibits.after: The size of the gear change surprised me. Artificial Analysis, an independent group that tests these models, ran the same Claude Opus 5.5 through its long set of hard tests at different settings. Thinking as hard as it can, it scored more than a third higher than when thinking a little. The older Opus 5, at its hardest, beat the new one at its lowest. OpenAI's GPT-6 Sol, which OpenAI's help page says powers ChatGPT's thinking settings, scored about two thirds higher at its top developer setting than with thinking off, while the newer GPT-6.1 Sol at its top only edged past it. In both cases the gear moved the score more than the new badge did.
exhibits.takeaway: On Artificial Analysis's 0 to 100 index, each line climbs 9.7 to 19.1 points from its lowest to its highest thinking level, while the newer version sits only 2.9 to 8.0 points above the older one at the same level, and mostly to its left, because it costs less to run.

exhibits.question: Is each step up in thinking level worth what it costs?
exhibits.heading: Each step up in thinking buys Claude and GPT less for every extra dollar
exhibits.after: It isn't a straight line, though, and that matters for where this is heading. Each step up buys less than the one before. On Artificial Analysis's tests, moving Opus 5.5 from low to medium cost about two and a half times as much per task and brought the biggest jump in its score. Moving it from medium to max cost another four and a half times as much, for a smaller jump. Bottom to top, that's about 11 times the cost for a score just over a third higher. Every current model from Anthropic and OpenAI on those tests works the same way: the top setting costs several times more than the bottom one, and the score goes up by far less. The last step up is the worst deal of all. On Fable 5.1, it costs 28% more and barely moves the score. And the setting can beat the model. Claude Haiku 5.5, the cheapest of Anthropic's current models, on its highest setting edged past Opus 5.5 on its lowest, for less than half the cost per task. Sometimes the top gear even scores lower than the one below it. On Hex's data-analysis test, GPT-6 Sol scored 61.3% on its Xhigh (extra high) setting and 57% on Max, which costs more. Thinking can be pure waste, too: researchers asked reasoning models "what is the answer of 2 plus 3?" and found they "consumed 1,953% more tokens than conventional models to reach the same answer." (Tokens are the word pieces an AI reads and writes, and what developers pay for.) One wrote out 13 solutions. And sometimes the new name really is the bigger step. Anthropic says Opus 5.5 on its default setting "beats Opus 5 at max effort for about a fifth of the cost" on one test of computer tasks.
exhibits.takeaway: On Artificial Analysis's 0 to 100 index, in all six, every step up added fewer points per extra dollar than the one before: Claude Opus 5.5's first step added 8.9 points for 2.4 times the cost, its last 1.6 points for 1.7 times.

exhibits.question: Which buys more intelligence for the money: a new model version or a higher thinking level?
exhibits.heading: A new Claude Opus or GPT Sol adds fewer points than more thinking, but costs less
exhibits.after: That's also why a higher gear eats into your plan faster. Anthropic's help page for the Claude app says higher effort means responses "take longer and use more tokens, so you'll reach your usage limits faster." Changing model can do the same, but not always. Anthropic charges developers two and a half times as much for the same amount of writing from Fable 5.1, the model it points them to when Opus 5.5 falls short, as from Opus 5.5. A newer version often costs less, as the Opus 5.5 example above shows.
exhibits.takeaway: On Artificial Analysis's 0 to 100 index, more thinking on the newest Claude Opus and GPT Sol added 9.7 to 15.3 points for 5.5 to 10.9 times the cost per task; the new version added 2.9 to 8.0 points at the same level and cost less at 9 of the 10 levels.

exhibits.question: If I need a given level of intelligence, which model and thinking level gets there cheapest, and where do the defaults land?
exhibits.heading: The cheapest route to each score mixes Claude and GPT models and thinking levels
exhibits.after: If you build products on AI, don't choose a model by its name or its launch chart. Run your own hard questions through each setting, check the answers, and watch how much thinking you pay for.
exhibits.takeaway: On Artificial Analysis's 0 to 100 index, scores up to 50 cost 12 to 32 cents a task at the cheapest; 55 takes Claude Opus 5.5 at Xhigh for $3.46, about 11 times as much, and Opus 5.5 on Anthropic's default (Medium) scores 51.2 for $1.34.
